lessons.title: Identify, authenticate, authorize, account
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a key ring with three objects: a "password" speech bubble, a phone and a fingerprint.
objectives: Tell apart identification, authentication, authorization and accountability (IAAA).
Place an authentication method in the right factor and recognize genuine MFA.
Interpret the error rates of a biometric system (FAR, FRR, CER).
Apply current recommendations on passwords and phishing-resistant MFA.

references.title: NIST SP 800-63B, Digital Identity Guidelines: authentication and authenticator lifecycle management

blocks.text: Four questions, in order

Every access to a system answers four successive questions. Who do you claim to be? Can you prove it? What are you allowed to do? What did you do? English-language textbooks call this IAAA: Identification, Authentication, Authorization, Accountability.

blocks.title: The IAAA chain
blocks.alt: Four-step diagram: identification (I claim an identity), authentication (I prove it), authorization (the system grants rights), accountability (my actions are logged and bind me).

nodes.label: Authorization
nodes.detail: what I am allowed to do

blocks.text: Accountability only exists if the identity is unique: a shared "admin" account breaks the chain.

blocks.title: Identification
blocks.text: Claiming an identity, for example typing a username or presenting a badge. On its own, it proves nothing.

blocks.title: Authentication
blocks.text: Checking that the claimed identity is the right one, using one or more factors.

blocks.title: Authorization (autorisation)
blocks.text: Deciding which resources and actions are allowed for an authenticated identity.

blocks.title: Accountability (traçabilité)
blocks.text: Being able to link every action to a person, thanks to unique identities and protected logs. It enables attribution and non-repudiation. Note: in governance, the same English word "accountability" means the ultimate accountability of management (see the Governance chapter).
In the exam, a question that talks about a "username" is about identification, not authentication. And a log without unique identities proves nothing: it is accountability that suffers.
Authentication factors

rows: Password, PIN code, answer to a question
FIDO2 security key, smart card, phone with an authenticator app

blocks.text: Some materials add context elements (location, time, typing behavior). They mainly serve to adjust the level of trust, for example in conditional access, rather than being a factor in their own right.

blocks.title: Genuine MFA or not?
blocks.text: Multi-factor authentication combines at least two factors from DIFFERENT categories. A password plus a PIN code are two knowledge elements: that is not MFA.
"KNOW, HAVE, ARE": something you KNOW, something you HAVE, something you ARE. Two different words = MFA; the same word twice = not MFA.
Biometrics and its errors

blocks.title: FRR, False Rejection Rate (taux de faux rejets), Type I error
blocks.text: Proportion of legitimate people wrongly refused. A high FRR annoys users.

blocks.title: FAR, False Acceptance Rate (taux de fausses acceptations), Type II error
blocks.text: Proportion of impostors wrongly accepted. It is the most dangerous error for security.

blocks.title: CER or EER, Crossover Error Rate (taux d'erreur égal)
blocks.text: Point where FAR and FRR are equal as the sensitivity is adjusted. The lower this rate, the more accurate the biometric system: it is the criterion for comparing products.

blocks.title: Tuning the sensitivity of a biometric reader
blocks.alt: Bar chart comparing two fictitious settings of a reader: lenient setting with 5 percent false acceptances and 2 percent false rejections; strict setting with 1 percent false acceptances and 6 percent false rejections.
blocks.text: Example figures: tightening the setting lowers the FAR but raises the FRR. You cannot reduce both at the same time.

blocks.title: Type I or Type II?
blocks.text: Type I = the Insider is wrongly refused (false rejection, FRR). Type II = the impostor gets through (false acceptance, FAR).
Passwords and MFA today

blocks.title: Current good practices
items: Favor length (passphrases) over arbitrary complexity rules.
Do not force periodic changes without a reason; change immediately in case of compromise.
Reject passwords already found in known breach lists.
Store passwords hashed with a salt and a slow algorithm designed for that purpose.
Prefer phishing-resistant MFA: FIDO2 keys or passkeys (WebAuthn).

blocks.title: Common attacks
items: Password spraying: a few common passwords tried against many accounts, to stay below the lockout thresholds.
Credential stuffing: username / password pairs stolen elsewhere, replayed against your services.
MFA fatigue: push notifications sent in bursts until the victim accepts.
Real-time phishing (adversary-in-the-middle): a fake site relays the password and the one-time code.

blocks.title: SOC case: 400 failures, 1 success
blocks.text: The SIEM reports 400 failed logins in ten minutes, spread over 380 different accounts, with a single password tried per account, from a few hosting-provider addresses. One account ends up succeeding. The analyst recognizes password spraying: no account was locked because each one suffered only a single attempt. The analyst kills the sessions of the compromised account, forces a password change, checks that no mail forwarding rule was created and proposes extending MFA to the accounts that did not have it.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: phishing-resistant MFA is my priority for privileged accounts and remote access.
SOC manager: I detect failures spread over many accounts, not only repeated failures on one account.
Auditor: I check that there are no shared accounts and that authentication logs are protected.
Risk manager: an Internet-facing account without MFA is a risk to treat first.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: Username = identification; password = authentication.
Two elements of the same factor do not make MFA.
FAR (Type II) is the most serious error for security; low CER = more accurate system.
Accountability requires unique identities: no shared accounts.
IAAA: identify, authenticate, authorize, account.
Factors: knowledge, possession, inherence; MFA = at least two different categories.
Biometrics: FRR (Type I), FAR (Type II), CER to compare.
Length, lists of compromised passwords, no forced rotation without a reason, phishing-resistant MFA.

lessons.title: Access control models
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of three doors of different colors with labels: a lock, a role badge and a "secret" label.
objectives: Tell apart DAC, MAC, RBAC, rule-based access control and ABAC.
Apply least privilege, need to know and implicit deny.
Remember the rules of the Bell-LaPadula (confidentiality) and Biba (integrity) models.

references.title: NIST SP 800-162, Guide to Attribute Based Access Control (ABAC)

blocks.text: Who decides on access?

rows: Access control lists (ACLs) the owner edits themselves
Sharing a Windows folder with a colleague
The system, according to a central policy
Classification labels on objects, clearances on subjects
Military systems, SELinux in strict mode
Rights are given to the role, people are given roles
"SOC analyst L1" role with read access to the SIEM
Rules that apply to everyone, regardless of identity
Combination of attributes of the subject, the resource, the action and the context
"The department's doctors, on duty, from a managed device"

blocks.text: The keyword that gives the model away: "owner" → DAC; "label" or "clearance" → MAC; "job" or "function" → RBAC; "firewall" or "time of day" → rules; "context" or "attributes" → ABAC.

blocks.title: An ABAC decision
blocks.alt: Five-step diagram: the attributes of the subject, the resource, the action and the context are sent to the policy decision point (PDP), which returns permit or deny to the policy enforcement point (PEP).

nodes.label: Decision
nodes.detail: the PDP decides, the PEP enforces

blocks.text: Principles that apply everywhere

blocks.title: Least privilege (moindre privilège)
blocks.text: Each identity receives only the rights strictly needed for its job, and only for as long as needed.

blocks.title: Need to know (besoin d'en connaître)
blocks.text: Even with a sufficient clearance, you only access information if your job requires it.

blocks.title: Implicit deny (refus par défaut)
blocks.text: Everything that is not explicitly allowed is forbidden. The last rule of a well-configured firewall denies everything else.
Two formal models to know

blocks.title: Bell-LaPadula or Biba?
blocks.text: Bell-LaPadula keeps secrets: you do not read above, you do not leak below. Biba is its mirror for integrity: you do not get dirty with what is below, you do not pollute what is above.

blocks.title: Key point
blocks.text: In a MAC model, users cannot share a resource on their own initiative, even if they created it. That is the essential difference with DAC.

blocks.title: Privilege creep
blocks.text: Without regular review, an employee who changes role keeps their old rights (privilege creep). RBAC limits this risk if roles are removed at every move.

blocks.title: SOC case: the role that is too broad
blocks.text: During an investigation, the SOC finds that an intern's account was able to read the HR folders. Cause: the "Head office user" role had given access to the HR share since an old migration. The SOC manager asks for the role to be revised (RBAC), for implicit deny to be applied on the share and for an access review by the owner of the HR data.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: I prefer RBAC because it is simple to review, complemented by ABAC for sensitive access.
SOC manager: my L1 analysts read the alerts; only L3 can isolate a server.
Auditor: I compare the actual rights with the approved roles.
Risk manager: every unnecessary right increases the impact of a compromised account.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: DAC: the owner decides; MAC: the system decides according to labels.
Rule-based access control is not RBAC (role-based).
Bell-LaPadula = confidentiality; Biba = integrity.
Need to know comes on top of clearance, it does not replace it.
DAC, MAC, RBAC, rules, ABAC: remember who decides.
Least privilege, need to know, implicit deny.
Bell-LaPadula: no read up, no write down. Biba: no read down, no write up.

lessons.title: Identity life cycle, SSO, federation and privileged access
lessons.illustrationAlt: Drawing of a central badge linked by arrows to three applications: a single badge opens several doors.
objectives: Describe the joiner, mover, leaver cycle and the access review.
Tell apart SSO, federation, SAML 2.0, OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect.
Explain how Kerberos works and its weak points.
Know the privileged access management (PAM) measures.

references.title: ISO/IEC 27002:2022, controls 5.16 (identity management), 5.18 (access rights) and 8.2 (privileged access rights)
RFC 4120, The Kerberos Network Authentication Service (V5)

blocks.text: Joiner, mover, leaver

blocks.title: The life cycle of an identity
blocks.alt: Four-step cycle: joiner (creation of the account and roles), mover (adding and removing rights), periodic access review, leaver (immediate deactivation), then back to the start for the next person.

blocks.text: This is the JML process (Joiner, Mover, Leaver). Automatic provisioning from the HR system reduces oversights: when the HR record changes, the rights follow.

blocks.title: Access review or recertification (revue des accès)
blocks.text: Periodic check in which the manager or the data owner confirms, or removes, each right held by their teams.
SSO and federation

blocks.title: Single sign-on, SSO (authentification unique)
blocks.text: A single authentication gives access to several applications. Convenient and fewer passwords, but a compromised account opens everything: MFA becomes essential.

blocks.title: Identity federation (fédération d'identités)
blocks.text: Trust relationship between organizations: an identity provider (IdP) authenticates the user, a service provider (SP) accepts its decision.

rows: An application accesses your files without knowing your password
Identity token (ID token, in JWT format)
"Sign in with…" on the web and on mobile

blocks.title: Key point
blocks.text: OAuth 2.0 is an authorization protocol, not an authentication protocol. To know WHO the user is, OpenID Connect is added on top.
SAML = "Signed Assertions for the enterprise". OAuth = "Authorize". OIDC = "OAuth + IDentity".
Kerberos

blocks.title: Kerberos in four steps
blocks.alt: Four-step diagram: the client authenticates to the authentication service (AS), which gives it a TGT; the client presents the TGT to the ticket-granting service (TGS), which gives it a service ticket; the client presents that ticket to the target server.
blocks.text: The KDC (key distribution center) combines the AS and the TGS. In Active Directory, these are the domain controllers.

blocks.title: Weak points of Kerberos
items: The KDC is a single point of failure and a prime target: it must be made redundant and protected.
Clocks must be synchronized: too large a gap makes authentication fail.
A stolen ticket can be replayed until it expires (pass-the-ticket attack).
Service accounts with a weak password expose their tickets to offline cracking (Kerberoasting).

blocks.text: Privileged access

blocks.title: PAM, Privileged Access Management measures
items: Administration accounts separate from office accounts.
Password vault with automatic rotation after use.
Just-in-time access: the right is granted for a limited time, after approval.
Recording of administration sessions and alerts sent to the SOC.
Dedicated administration workstations and phishing-resistant MFA.

blocks.text: In almost every serious intrusion, the attacker looks for a privileged account. A SOC that monitors administrator logins (unusual time, new device, new country) often detects the attack before the encryption.

blocks.title: SOC case: impossible travel
blocks.text: An administrator's account logs in from Lyon at 9:02, then from another continent at 9:15. No plane makes that trip in 13 minutes: it is an "impossible travel" alert. The analyst checks the device and token used, revokes the active sessions and tokens, resets the password and MFA factors, then looks for any account creation or rights change since 9:15.

blocks.title: Points of view
items: CISO: SSO with strong MFA for everyone, PAM for administrators, quarterly review of sensitive access.
SOC manager: the logs of the IdP and of the domain controllers are my most valuable sources.
Auditor: I check that every HR departure led to the account being disabled, with the date.
Risk manager: the identity provider concentrates risk; its availability and security are critical.

blocks.title: Exam pitfalls
items: OAuth 2.0 authorizes, OpenID Connect authenticates.
SAML exchanges XML assertions; OIDC exchanges JWT tokens.
Kerberos: TGT issued by the AS, service ticket issued by the TGS.
When an employee leaves, the account is disabled immediately, not necessarily deleted at once (logs and data may be needed).
Joiner, mover, leaver, and regular access review.
SSO = one authentication, several applications; federation = trust between IdP and SP.
SAML (assertions), OAuth 2.0 (delegated authorization), OIDC (identity).
Kerberos: KDC, AS, TGS, tickets, synchronized clocks.
PAM: separate accounts, vault, just-in-time, recorded sessions.

questions.prompt: A user types their username "j.martin" on the login page. Which step are they performing?
questions.explanation: Claiming an identity, without proving it, is identification.

whyNot.0: Accountability then links their actions to their identity.
whyNot.1: Authorization comes later, when the system decides on their rights.
whyNot.2: Authentication starts when they prove the identity, for example with their password.

questions.prompt: A FIDO2 security key plugged in via USB belongs to which factor?
questions.explanation: The key is an object the user holds: it is a possession factor.

whyNot.0: Inherence covers biometric characteristics.
whyNot.2: Location is a context element, not the factor of this key.
whyNot.3: Knowledge covers memorized secrets (password, PIN).

questions.prompt: Which of these combinations is genuine multifactor authentication?
questions.explanation: MFA combines factors from different categories: knowledge (password) and inherence (fingerprint).

whyNot.0: Two passwords are still a single factor, knowledge.
whyNot.1: The security question is also a knowledge element.
whyNot.2: Password and PIN are two knowledge elements.

questions.prompt: A fingerprint reader lets in an unregistered person. What type of error has occurred?
choices: A false rejection (FRR, type I error)
The equal error rate (CER, or EER)
An error that occurred during enrollment
questions.explanation: Accepting an impostor is a false acceptance, the type II error, the most dangerous for security.

whyNot.0: A false rejection refuses a legitimate person.
whyNot.1: The CER is the point where FAR and FRR are equal, not a one-off error.
whyNot.3: Enrollment is the initial registration of fingerprints; that is not what happened here.

questions.prompt: To compare the accuracy of two biometric readers, which indicator is used?
questions.explanation: The equal error rate sums up accuracy: the lower it is, the more accurate the system.

whyNot.0: A high FRR means many rejections of legitimate users.
whyNot.1: A high FAR means many impostors accepted.
whyNot.3: Speed is a convenience criterion, not an accuracy one.

questions.prompt: Which measure complies with current password recommendations (for example NIST SP 800-63B)?
choices: Rejecting passwords found in known breach lists
Requiring an uppercase letter, a digit and a symbol whatever the length
Sending a password hint by email
questions.explanation: Current recommendations favor length and rejecting compromised or overly common passwords.

whyNot.1: Arbitrary composition rules are discouraged in favor of length.
whyNot.2: Periodic changes without reason lead to predictable passwords; passwords are changed upon compromise.
whyNot.3: Hints make the attacker's job easier.

questions.prompt: Which authentication methods best resist a phishing site that relays the login in real time? (2 answers)
choices: Passkey (WebAuthn) bound to the domain name
questions.explanation: FIDO2 and passkeys bind the signature to the real domain name: a fake site cannot obtain a valid response for the real one.

whyNot.1: An app code can also be relayed by the attacker while it is valid.
whyNot.3: An SMS code can be entered on the fake site and relayed immediately.

questions.prompt: The SIEM shows a single password attempt on each of 500 accounts, from the same source, within a few minutes. What is this?
choices: A brute-force attack on a single account
questions.explanation: Few attempts on many accounts, to stay under lockout thresholds: this is spraying.

whyNot.1: MFA fatigue consists of sending bursts of push notifications.
whyNot.2: Brute force targets one account with many attempts.
whyNot.3: Ticket replay does not involve password attempts.

questions.prompt: Why are shared accounts ("admin" used by five people) a problem?
choices: They are forbidden by all operating systems
They prevent attributing an action to a person
questions.explanation: Without a unique identity, logs cannot show who did what: accountability is lost.

whyNot.0: Sharing has no effect on speed.
whyNot.1: Backups do not depend on this.
whyNot.2: Systems allow it technically; it is a bad practice.

questions.prompt: A user reports dozens of MFA notifications they did not request. Which measures reduce this risk? (2 answers)
choices: Enabling number matching (typing the number shown on screen)
Limiting the number of notifications and alerting the SOC beyond a threshold
questions.explanation: Number matching prevents reflex approval, and limiting with an alert stops and reports the burst.

whyNot.2: Longer sessions do not prevent the attack and extend the use of a stolen session.
whyNot.3: Removing MFA would leave the account protected only by the password, which the attacker already has.

questions.prompt: An employee shares her folder with a colleague herself by changing the permissions. Which model is at work?
questions.explanation: In discretionary access control (DAC), the owner decides the rights on their resources.

whyNot.0: In RBAC, rights follow the roles defined by the organization.
whyNot.2: Rule-based control applies global rules, like a firewall.
whyNot.3: In MAC, the system enforces access according to labels; the user cannot share freely.

questions.prompt: In which model are rights assigned to functions such as "accountant" or "tier 1 SOC analyst"?
questions.explanation: RBAC assigns rights to roles, then roles to people.

whyNot.0: ABAC combines attributes; a role can be one of them, but the model described here is RBAC.
whyNot.1: DAC lets the owner decide.
whyNot.3: MAC relies on classification labels.

questions.prompt: A military system compares a document's "Secret" label with the user's clearance, and the user cannot change anything. Which model?
questions.explanation: Mandatory access control (MAC) enforces access according to labels and clearances defined centrally.

whyNot.1: RBAC reasons in roles, not in classification levels.
whyNot.2: In DAC, the owner could change the rights.
whyNot.3: Rule-based control applies general rules without comparing clearance and classification.

questions.prompt: "Cardiology department doctors can read their patients' records, while on duty, from a managed device." Which model best expresses this rule?
questions.explanation: The rule combines attributes of the subject (job, department), the resource (patient) and the context (time, device): this is ABAC.

whyNot.0: No owner decides case by case here.
whyNot.1: Classification labels are not involved.
whyNot.2: RBAC alone cannot take time or device into account.

questions.prompt: An analyst cleared "Confidential" requests a "Confidential" file from an investigation they are not part of. Which principle justifies the refusal?
questions.explanation: The clearance is sufficient, but their mission does not require it: this is need to know.

whyNot.0: Least privilege concerns the extent of the rights granted; here the deciding criterion is the link with the mission.
whyNot.1: Default deny concerns what is not explicitly allowed.
whyNot.2: Separation of duties splits a sensitive task among several people.

questions.prompt: Which model protects confidentiality with the rules "no read up, no write down"?
questions.explanation: Bell-LaPadula prevents reading above one's level and copying information down to a lower level.

whyNot.0: Brewer-Nash (Chinese Wall) prevents conflicts of interest.
whyNot.1: Clark-Wilson protects integrity through well-formed transactions and separation of duties.
whyNot.2: Biba protects integrity with the opposite rules.

questions.prompt: In the Biba model, which statements are correct? (2 answers)
choices: It forbids reading data at a lower integrity level
It forbids reading data at a higher level
questions.explanation: Biba protects integrity: no read down, no write up.

whyNot.0: Confidentiality is the purpose of Bell-LaPadula.
whyNot.2: Forbidding reading up is a Bell-LaPadula rule.

questions.prompt: A firewall's last rule blocks all traffic not allowed by a previous rule. Which principle is applied?
questions.explanation: Everything not explicitly permitted is forbidden: this is default deny (implicit deny).

whyNot.1: Job rotation concerns staff.
whyNot.2: Defense in depth stacks several layers of protection.
whyNot.3: Need to know concerns a person's access to information.

questions.prompt: After three department changes, an employee keeps all their former rights. Which measure best fixes this problem?
choices: An access review and removal of rights at each transfer
Increasing their password length and enabling MFA
Giving them a unique, named administrator role
Enabling full disk encryption on their workstation
questions.explanation: Privilege accumulation is handled by removing rights at transfers and through regular reviews.

whyNot.1: The password has no effect on the extent of rights.
whyNot.2: An administrator role would make the problem worse.
whyNot.3: Encryption protects data at rest, not access rights.

questions.prompt: Which statement correctly distinguishes rule-based control from role-based control?
choices: Rule-based control lets the resource owner decide the rights
Rule-based control compares classification labels with clearances
Rule-based control applies the same rules to everyone, whatever their function
They are two different names for the same model
questions.explanation: Rule-based control (firewall, time windows) applies the same rules to everyone; RBAC depends on the function.

whyNot.0: That is the principle of DAC.
whyNot.1: Labels characterize MAC.
whyNot.3: The two acronyms look alike (RBAC), but the models are different.

questions.prompt: Which protocol is designed to delegate authorization, for example letting an application access your files without knowing your password?
questions.explanation: OAuth 2.0 issues access tokens that represent a delegated authorization.

whyNot.0: Kerberos authenticates within a domain using tickets.
whyNot.1: LDAP is a directory access protocol.
whyNot.3: SAML 2.0 is mainly used for authentication and federation through XML assertions.

questions.prompt: Which protocol adds an authentication layer (identity token) on top of OAuth 2.0?
questions.explanation: OpenID Connect builds on OAuth 2.0 and provides an ID token, in JWT format, that describes the authenticated user.

whyNot.0: RADIUS is a network authentication protocol, unrelated to OAuth.
whyNot.2: Kerberos works with tickets, not on top of OAuth.
whyNot.3: SAML 2.0 is a separate standard, based on XML.

questions.prompt: In a SAML federation, which party authenticates the user and issues the assertion?
questions.explanation: The identity provider authenticates the user and issues a signed assertion that the service provider accepts.

whyNot.1: The SP consumes the assertion; it does not issue it.
whyNot.2: The firewall plays no part in SAML.
whyNot.3: The browser often carries the assertion but does not issue it.

questions.prompt: In Kerberos, which component issues the ticket-granting ticket (TGT)?
questions.explanation: The client authenticates to the AS, which gives it the TGT; it will then present this TGT to the TGS.

whyNot.0: The TGS issues service tickets in exchange for the TGT.
whyNot.1: The client requests tickets; it does not issue them.
whyNot.3: The file server receives a service ticket; it does not issue any.

questions.prompt: A workstation's clock and the domain controller's clock are 20 minutes apart. What is the likely consequence with Kerberos?
choices: Authentication fails, because tickets are timestamped
The workstation takes over the domain controller role
The user's password is sent in cleartext
questions.explanation: Kerberos timestamps its exchanges to limit replay; beyond the configured tolerance, authentication is refused.

whyNot.1: Time is, on the contrary, essential to Kerberos.
whyNot.2: A clock skew does not change a machine's role.
whyNot.3: Kerberos does not send the password over the network.

questions.prompt: Which statements about Kerberos weaknesses are correct? (2 answers)
choices: A stolen ticket can be replayed until it expires
The KDC is a single point of failure that should be made redundant
questions.explanation: The KDC concentrates trust and availability; a stolen ticket remains usable while it is valid (pass-the-ticket).

whyNot.2: Kerberos does not require any particular factor.
whyNot.3: The password is used to derive a key; it does not travel in cleartext.

questions.prompt: An administrator leaves the company tonight. Which action is the priority?
choices: Disabling their accounts and revoking their access and sessions as soon as they leave
Waiting for the next quarterly access review
Immediately deleting all their data and mailbox
questions.explanation: Immediately disabling the accounts and revoking sessions closes access; data is retained according to the applicable rules.

whyNot.0: Guest Wi-Fi is not an administrator's most critical access.
whyNot.2: Waiting for the review leaves an active account without an owner.
whyNot.3: Deleting everything right away can destroy useful data or evidence.

questions.prompt: Which measure belongs to privileged access management (PAM)?
choices: An antivirus with behavioral analysis on workstations
A clean desk and locked screen policy
An administrator password vault with rotation after use
A weekly backup of administration servers
questions.explanation: The vault, just-in-time access and session recording are typical PAM measures.

whyNot.0: Antivirus protects against malware.
whyNot.1: Clean desk is a physical and organizational security measure.
whyNot.3: Backup relates to availability.

questions.prompt: What are the effects of SSO on security? (2 answers)
choices: It removes the need for authentication
Fewer passwords to remember, so less reuse
A compromised account gives access to all connected applications
questions.explanation: SSO reduces password fatigue but concentrates risk on a single authentication, which must therefore be strong.

whyNot.0: The user still authenticates, just once.
whyNot.2: MFA becomes, on the contrary, essential on the SSO account.

questions.prompt: The same account logs in from Paris and then, 10 minutes later, from another continent. Which detection is triggered?
questions.explanation: Two logins too far apart for such a short time indicate impossible travel: credentials or tokens were probably stolen.

whyNot.0: Kerberoasting targets service account tickets.
whyNot.1: Spraying targets many accounts with few attempts each.
whyNot.2: MFA fatigue shows up as bursts of notifications.

flashcards.back: Identification, authentication, authorization, accountability.
Claiming an identity (username, badge). It proves nothing.
Proving the claimed identity with one or more factors.
Knowledge (something you know), possession (something you have), inherence (something you are).
At least two factors from different categories.
False rejection: a legitimate person is refused.
False acceptance: an impostor is accepted. The most serious error.
The point where FAR = FRR. The lower it is, the more accurate the system.
A few common passwords tried against many accounts.
FIDO2 / passkeys (WebAuthn), bound to the real domain name.
The owner decides (ACL).
The system decides based on labels and clearances.
Rights assigned to roles, roles assigned to people.
Decision based on attributes of the subject, the resource, the action and the context.
Confidentiality: no read up, no write down.
Integrity: no read down, no write up.
OAuth authorizes (access token). OIDC authenticates (JWT ID token) on top of OAuth.
Signed XML assertions issued by the IdP for the SP.
AS → TGT; TGS → service ticket; synchronized clocks.
Separate admin accounts, vault, just-in-time access, recorded sessions.

revisionSheet: # Revision sheet: IAM, authentication and access control
IAAA: identification (claim) → authentication (prove) → authorization (rights) → accountability (logs, unique identities).
Factors: knowledge, possession, inherence. MFA = at least two different categories.
Biometrics: FRR = Type I (wrongly refused); FAR = Type II (impostor accepted, the most serious); low CER/EER = more accurate.
Passwords: length, rejecting compromised passwords, no forced rotation without a reason, slow salted hashing.
Phishing-resistant MFA: FIDO2, passkeys. Against MFA fatigue: number matching, rate limiting and alerting.
Attacks: brute force, password spraying, credential stuffing, MFA fatigue, real-time phishing.
Models: DAC (owner), MAC (labels), RBAC (roles), rule-based (firewall, time of day), ABAC (attributes, PDP/PEP).
Principles: least privilege, need to know, default deny, separation of duties.
Bell-LaPadula (confidentiality): no read up, no write down. Biba (integrity): no read down, no write up.
Life cycle: joiner, mover, leaver (JML) + access reviews; disable immediately on departure.
SSO (one authentication, several applications); federation (IdP ↔ SP); SAML (XML assertions); OAuth 2.0 (authorization); OIDC (identity, JWT).
Kerberos: KDC = AS + TGS; TGT, then service ticket; synchronized clocks; pass-the-ticket and Kerberoasting risks.
PAM: separate accounts, vault, rotation, just-in-time, recorded sessions.
Pairs not to confuse: identification/authentication; FAR/FRR; DAC/MAC; rule-based/role-based; Bell-LaPadula/Biba; OAuth/OIDC; AS/TGS.
